tool.name: seaborn
tool.tagline: Statistical data visualization on top of Matplotlib and pandas
tool.description: seaborn is a high-level plotting library that turns pandas DataFrames into informative statistical charts in one call: distributions, relationships, categorical comparisons, regressions and multi-panel facets, with sensible themes and color palettes. Because it draws on Matplotlib, every chart can be fine-tuned with Matplotlib when needed.

glossary.def: A job a column is given in a seaborn chart, such as where points sit (x, y), their color (hue), marker shape (style) or size. seaborn turns the column's values into that visual.
seaborn's name for the color role: the column whose values decide the color of each point, line or bar.
A table with one row per observation and one column per kind of information, e.g. columns year, city, sales with a row for each city in each year. seaborn's preferred input.
A table where one kind of information is spread across many columns, e.g. a year column and then one column per city. Easy for people to read; seaborn usually wants long-form instead.
Describes a column whose values name groups (city, plan, species) rather than measure amounts. pandas also has a special category type for such columns.
The set of colors seaborn uses for the groups or values in a chart, picked by name ("deep", "colorblind", "mako") or given as a list or dict.
A palette of clearly different colors with no order, for categories such as cities or plans.
A palette that goes from light to dark (or one color to another) in steps, for amounts where more means darker.
A palette with a neutral color in the middle and two different colors getting stronger toward each end, for values above and below a center such as zero.
seaborn's setting for where a chart will be seen (paper, notebook, talk, poster); it scales fonts and line widths to suit.
One of the four lines that frame a plot area (top, bottom, left, right); the ticks sit on the bottom and left ones.
How a variable's values are spread out: which values are common, which are rare, where the middle lies and how far they stretch.
How tightly values are packed at each point of the number line, scaled so the whole area under the curve (or of the bars) is 1. High density means many values there.
Kernel density estimate: a smooth curve showing where values are common, made by placing a small bump on every data point and adding the bumps up. A smooth alternative to a histogram.
In a KDE, the small bump (usually bell-shaped) placed on each data point; adding all the bumps together gives the smooth curve.
In a KDE, how wide each bump is: a wider bandwidth gives a smoother curve, a narrower one shows more detail and more noise.
A step line that shows, for every value, what share of the data is at or below it. It climbs from 0 to 1 and needs no bins.
A line joining points of equal value, like the height lines on a hiking map; in a two-variable KDE it rings the areas where data is densest.
The three values that cut sorted data into four equal-sized parts. The middle one is the median; the middle half of the data lies between the first and third quartile.
Interquartile range: the distance from the first to the third quartile, i.e. the width of the middle half of the data.
A chart that summarizes a group with a box from the first to the third quartile, a line at the median and whiskers out to the typical extremes; values beyond are drawn as single dots.
In a box plot, the line reaching out from the box to the furthest value that is still within 1.5 times the box's height (the IQR).
A chart that draws each group's KDE curve on its side, mirrored, so the shape shows where the group's values bunch up.
A chart with one dot per value for each category, nudged sideways a little at random so equal values don't hide each other.
Like a strip plot, but the dots are packed side by side so that none of them overlap.
A small random sideways shift added to each dot so dots with the same value don't sit exactly on top of each other.
Placing sub-groups side by side within one category (for example a bar per plan inside each region) instead of on top of each other.
A range that very likely contains the true value of an estimate, such as a group's mean, given the data you have. A 95% interval is built to succeed 95% of the time; more data makes it narrower.
In statistics, how much an estimate such as a mean would typically change if you collected the data again: roughly the standard deviation divided by the square root of the number of values.
A line or shaded band drawn around an estimate to show how uncertain it is or how spread out the data is. Always say which one it shows.
In seaborn, the function that summarizes several values into one number, such as the mean (the default) or the median.
A way to measure uncertainty: redraw your rows at random (repeats allowed) many times, recompute the statistic each time, and see how much the results vary.
In statistics, drawing a new set of rows of the same size from your own data at random, where a row may be picked more than once. The bootstrap does this many times.
Data where the same subject (a person, a machine) is measured several times, so its rows are related to each other rather than independent.
A seaborn function such as scatterplot or boxplot that draws onto one existing Matplotlib Axes and returns it.
A seaborn function such as relplot or displot that creates a whole new figure, possibly with many panels, and returns a grid object that manages it.
To split a chart into a grid of small panels, one per value of a column (one per region, say), all drawn the same way. Each panel is also called a facet.
The seaborn object behind relplot, displot, catplot and lmplot: a figure with one panel (Axes) per subset of the data, plus helpers for titles, labels and the legend.
The seaborn object behind pairplot: a grid with one panel for every pair of chosen columns.
The seaborn object behind jointplot: one main two-variable plot with a small one-variable plot along its top and right edges.
A small chart along the edge of a two-variable plot showing how one of the two variables is spread out on its own.
A grid of colored cells in which each cell's color shows a number, like a table you read by color.
A way to order rows (or columns) by similarity: repeatedly join the two most similar ones into a group until everything is in one tree.
Fitting the line (or curve) that best predicts one variable from another, such as sales from ad spend.
The gap between an actual value and the value a fitted line predicts for it.
A formula built from powers of x, such as 3 + 2x + 0.5x²; adding the x² part lets a fitted line bend into a curve.
A regression for a yes/no (0/1) outcome: it fits an S-shaped curve giving the chance of "yes" at each x.
A smooth curve fitted through a scatter plot by averaging nearby points along x, without assuming any formula for its shape.
A number from 0 to 1 saying how surprising your result would be if there were really no effect; small values suggest the effect is real.
A Python library for statistical models and tests: it fits regressions and reports their numbers, such as slopes and p-values.
A Python library of scientific math built on NumPy: statistics, optimization, clustering and more.
A Python library for machine learning: training models that learn patterns from data and make predictions.
seaborn's newer way to build charts: start from a Plot object and add layers, each made of a mark, an optional stat and optional moves.
The idea that any chart can be described as data plus layers: what shape to draw, how values become positions and colors, and what calculation to apply first.
In seaborn.objects, an object that decides what is drawn for the data: dots, lines, bars, bands, text and so on.
In seaborn.objects, an object that computes new data before it is drawn, such as the mean per group or histogram counts.
In seaborn.objects, an object that shifts marks so they don't collide, for example placing bars side by side or stacking them.
In seaborn.objects, a visual quality a mark can have, such as its x or y position, color, size, line width or marker shape.

concepts.name: seaborn and long-form data
concepts.summary: How seaborn turns DataFrame columns into parts of a chart (position, color, shape) and why it wants one row per observation.
concepts.why: Nearly every seaborn call takes `data=` plus column names, so getting the table into the right shape is most of the work.
concepts.body:
Drawing a chart by groups in plain Matplotlib takes many small steps: split the rows by group, pick a color for each, draw them one by one, then build the legend. **seaborn** is a library that does those steps for you. You hand it a pandas DataFrame and say which column goes where; it works out the groups, colors and legend, then draws with **Matplotlib** underneath. The usual import is `import seaborn as sns`.

A typical call is `sns.scatterplot(data=df, x="height", y="weight", hue="sex")`. Each keyword gives a column a job in the picture, called a **semantic role**: where each point sits (`x`, `y`), its color (`hue`, seaborn's word for color), its marker shape (`style`) or its `size`. Later lessons add `col` and `row`, which split a chart into several panels.

seaborn works best with **long-form** data: one row per observation (one measurement of one thing) and one column per variable (one kind of information, such as year, city or sales). Columns `year`, `city` and `sales`, with a row for each city in each year, are long-form.

A table with a `year` column and then one column per city is **wide-form**. It is easy for people to read, but the city names are only column headers, so there is no `city` column you could give a role to.

To turn wide into long, use the DataFrame method `melt`: `wide.melt(id_vars="year", var_name="city", value_name="sales")`. The `id_vars` columns stay as they are; every other column is stacked into two new ones, one holding the old header (`city`) and one holding the number (`sales`). Long-form is what lets you give any column any role.

seaborn functions return the Matplotlib object they drew on, usually an Axes, so you add titles and save exactly as in Matplotlib: `ax.set_title(...)`, then `ax.figure.savefig("plot.png")` (`ax.figure` is the Figure holding that Axes).

seaborn also ships small example **datasets** (ready-made tables) for practice, loaded with `sns.load_dataset("tips")`. They are downloaded from the internet, so code that must work offline should build its own DataFrame.

Finally, seaborn looks at what a column holds. Numbers are treated as amounts: a numeric axis, and a gradual range of shades for `hue`. Text such as city names is treated as **categorical**: each value names a group, and each group gets its own clearly different color.
concepts.code:
import matplotlib
matplotlib.use("Agg")                   # draw to files only, no window
import seaborn as sns
import pandas as pd

wide = pd.DataFrame({"year": [2024, 2025, 2026],
                     "Paris": [10, 12, 15], "Lyon": [7, 9, 8]})
# keep "year"; stack the city columns into "city" (header) and "sales" (number)
long = wide.melt(id_vars="year", var_name="city", value_name="sales")
print(long.shape)                       # (6, 3)
print(long.columns.tolist())            # ['year', 'city', 'sales']

ax = sns.lineplot(data=long, x="year", y="sales", hue="city", marker="o")
ax.set_title("Sales by city")
print(type(ax).__name__)                # Axes
print([t.get_text() for t in ax.get_legend().get_texts()])  # ['Paris', 'Lyon']
ax.figure.savefig("sales.png")
takeaways: Pass `data=df` and give columns roles: x, y, hue, style, size, col, row
Prefer long-form data (one row per observation); reshape wide tables with `melt`
Functions return Matplotlib objects you can keep customizing
pitfalls: Passing a wide table and writing `hue="city"`: the city names are only column headers, so there is no `city` column for seaborn to use.

quiz.q: Your DataFrame has columns 'date', 'north', 'south', 'east' with sales per region. What do you do before `sns.lineplot(..., hue='region')`?
options: Swap its rows and columns with df.T
Convert it to a NumPy array
Melt it so there is a 'region' column and a single value column
quiz.explain: hue needs one column whose values are the regions; melting the wide table creates that column.

concepts.name: Scatter and line plots with semantics
concepts.summary: Use scatterplot and lineplot with hue, style and size to show how two variables relate, for each group.
concepts.why: Showing a relationship split by group in one call, legend included, is seaborn's core time-saver.
concepts.body:
A scatter plot draws one dot per row; a line plot joins the points up. In seaborn these are `sns.scatterplot` and `sns.lineplot`, the relational plots, because they show how one variable relates to another. Beyond `x` and `y`, both take three more roles:

- `hue`: color. A categorical column gets a set of clearly different colors, a **palette**; a numeric column gets a gradual range of shades (a colormap).
- `style`: marker shape for dots, or dash pattern for lines; always treated as categories.
- `size`: dot size or line width, usually for a numeric column; set the smallest and largest with `sizes=(20, 200)`.

Giving the same column to both `hue` and `style` makes each group differ in color *and* shape. That repetition keeps the chart readable when printed in gray or seen by a color-blind reader.

Groups get their colors, and their place in the legend, in the order they first appear in the data. Pass `hue_order=["Lima", "Oslo", "Rome"]` to fix the order, so a city keeps the same color from chart to chart.

`lineplot` sorts rows by `x` before joining the points, so unsorted input is fine. If several rows share the same `x`, it combines them: the line goes through their mean, and a shaded band shows how uncertain that mean is. The aggregation lesson explains the band and how to change it.

`legend="brief"` (the default for a numeric hue) lists a few sample values, `"full"` lists every value and `False` hides the legend. To reposition it, call `sns.move_legend(ax, "upper left", bbox_to_anchor=(1, 1))`: the legend's upper-left corner goes to the top-right corner of the Axes, just outside the plot.

With thousands of dots, overplotting hides where the data is dense. Make dots see-through (`alpha=0.3`) or smaller (`s=5`), or switch to a 2D histogram with `sns.histplot(x=..., y=...)`, which counts the points in a grid of small squares and colors each square by its count.
concepts.code:
import matplotlib
matplotlib.use("Agg")
import seaborn as sns
import pandas as pd
import numpy as np

rng = np.random.default_rng(0)          # random numbers; seed 0 makes them repeat
n = 120
df = pd.DataFrame({
    "area": rng.uniform(30, 150, n),
    "city": rng.choice(["Oslo", "Rome", "Lima"], n),
    "rooms": rng.integers(1, 6, n),
})
df["price"] = df["area"] * 4 + df["rooms"] * 20 + rng.normal(0, 40, n)

ax = sns.scatterplot(data=df, x="area", y="price", hue="city", style="city",
                     size="rooms", sizes=(20, 160),
                     hue_order=["Lima", "Oslo", "Rome"], alpha=0.8)
sns.move_legend(ax, "upper left", bbox_to_anchor=(1, 1))   # just outside, top right
texts = [t.get_text() for t in ax.get_legend().get_texts()]
print(texts[:4])            # ['city', 'Lima', 'Oslo', 'Rome']
ax.figure.savefig("homes.png", bbox_inches="tight")
takeaways: `hue`, `style` and `size` add up to three extra variables to a scatter or line plot
Fix the group order with `hue_order` so colors stay the same across charts
Use `sns.move_legend` to reposition seaborn legends
pitfalls: Giving `hue` a column with hundreds of different values (such as user ids), which produces hundreds of colors and an unreadable legend.

quiz.q: You give the same 'species' column to both hue and style. What is the benefit?
options: It is required when using style
Groups stay distinguishable without color, e.g. in grayscale or for color-blind readers
quiz.explain: Each group then differs in both color and marker shape, so the groups stay readable even when the colors are not.

concepts.name: Distributions: histplot, kdeplot, ecdfplot
concepts.summary: Show how a variable's values are spread out with histograms, smooth KDE curves and ECDFs, overall and per group.
concepts.why: Seeing how values are spread out comes before any modeling, and these functions compare groups in one line.
concepts.body:
A variable's **distribution** is how its values are spread out: which values are common, which are rare, where the middle is and how far they stretch. seaborn has three functions for looking at it.

`histplot` draws a histogram: it splits the number line into bins and counts the values in each. Key options:

- `bins=` (how many) or `binwidth=` (how wide); the default picks a sensible count.
- `stat=` sets the bar height: `"count"` (default), `"percent"`, `"probability"` (shares adding up to 1) or `"density"`.
- `hue=` splits by group, and `multiple=` decides how groups combine: `"layer"` (overlapping, the default), `"stack"`, `"dodge"` (side by side) or `"fill"` (each group's share of every bin).
- `common_norm=False` scales each group on its own, so a small group isn't flattened next to a big one.
- `kde=True` adds a smooth curve over the bars.

**Density** scales the bars so their total area is 1. A small and a large group then end up on the same scale, which makes their shapes easy to compare.

`kdeplot` draws that smooth curve on its own, called a **KDE** (kernel density estimate). Picture a small bell-shaped bump, the **kernel**, placed on every data point; adding all the bumps up gives the curve. High parts mean many values there.

How wide each bump is, the **bandwidth**, sets how smooth the curve looks. `bw_adjust` scales it: below 1 shows more detail (and more noise), above 1 smooths more. Because bumps spill past the data, a KDE can suggest impossible values, such as negative prices; `cut=0` stops the curve at the smallest and largest values.

`ecdfplot` draws an **ECDF**: a step line giving, for each value, the share of the data at or below it. It needs no bins or bandwidth, so it hides nothing. Reading off a **percentile** is easy: where the line reaches 0.9 is the 90th percentile, the value 90% of the data is below (0.5 gives the median).

Given both `x` and `y`, `histplot` and `kdeplot` show two variables at once: as a grid of colored squares, or as **contour** lines, like the height lines on a hiking map, ringing the areas where points are densest.

`displot(kind="hist")` (or `"kde"`, `"ecdf"`) draws the same plots split into panels, one per group, with `col=` and `row=`; a later lesson covers it.
concepts.code:
import matplotlib
matplotlib.use("Agg")
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt
import seaborn as sns
import pandas as pd
import numpy as np

rng = np.random.default_rng(1)
eu = rng.lognormal(3, 0.4, 900)         # 900 response times in ms: positive, long right tail
us = rng.lognormal(3.6, 0.3, 100)       # 100 slower ones
df = pd.DataFrame({"latency": list(eu) + list(us),
                   "region": ["eu"] * 900 + ["us"] * 100})

fig, (a, b, c) = plt.subplots(1, 3, figsize=(12, 3.5), layout="constrained")
sns.histplot(data=df, x="latency", hue="region", stat="density",
             common_norm=False, ax=a)
sns.kdeplot(data=df, x="latency", hue="region", common_norm=False,
            bw_adjust=0.7, cut=0, ax=b)
sns.ecdfplot(data=df, x="latency", hue="region", ax=c)

for r in ["eu", "us"]:
    print(r, round(df[df["region"] == r]["latency"].median(), 1))
# eu 19.9
# us 35.8
fig.savefig("latency.png")
takeaways: histplot for counts, kdeplot for a smooth shape, ecdfplot for reading percentiles exactly
Use `common_norm=False` when comparing groups of very different sizes
Bin count and `bw_adjust` change the picture; try a few values
pitfalls: Trusting the ends of a KDE curve as real data, for example a curve below zero for a value that is never negative.

quiz.q: Group A has 10,000 rows and group B has 200. With `sns.histplot(..., hue='group', stat='density')` group B's bars look tiny. Why?
options: By default the density is scaled across all groups together (common_norm=True)
B needs a separate bins value
quiz.explain: With common_norm=True the bars of all groups together have an area of 1, so the small group gets a small share; set common_norm=False.

concepts.name: Categorical plots: box, violin, bar, strip
concepts.summary: Compare a number across groups with strip, swarm, box, violin, bar, point and count plots.
concepts.why: Comparing groups, such as two versions of a web page, several regions or several products, is one of the most common analysis tasks.
concepts.body:
Many questions compare groups: is version B of a page faster than A? seaborn's categorical plots put the groups along one axis and a number along the other. They come in three families.

**Show every value.** A **strip plot** (`stripplot`) draws one dot per row, each nudged sideways a little at random (**jitter**) so equal values don't hide each other. A **swarm plot** (`swarmplot`) instead packs the dots so none overlap; it works well up to a few hundred per group.

**Show the spread.** A **box plot** (`boxplot`) summarizes each group. Sort the values and cut them into four equal-sized parts: the three cut points are the **quartiles**, and the middle one is the median. The box runs from the first to the third quartile, so it holds the middle half of the data; its height is the **IQR** (interquartile range).

The box plot's **whiskers** reach out to the furthest values that are no more than 1.5 × IQR beyond the box; anything beyond is drawn as a single dot, a possible outlier. A **violin plot** (`violinplot`) instead draws each group's KDE curve on its side, mirrored, so you see where values bunch up. `boxenplot` shows more, narrower boxes and suits large data.

**Show an estimate.** `barplot` draws each group's mean as a bar, with a thin line on top, an **error bar**, showing how uncertain that mean is. By default it is a 95% **confidence interval**: a range that very likely contains the true mean, the one you would get with endless data. More data makes it shorter. `pointplot` shows the same as dots joined by lines, and `countplot` simply counts rows per category.

Put the categories on `x` for vertical plots or on `y` for horizontal ones. `order=[...]` sets their order, and `hue=` splits each category by a second column, placing the sub-groups side by side (seaborn calls this **dodge**). Plots can be layered: a box plot and a strip plot on the same `ax` show the summary and the raw data together.

A bar of the mean hides how spread out the values are, so prefer box, violin or dots when that matters. And give `barplot` the raw rows, not values you already averaged, or there is nothing left to measure uncertainty from.

In seaborn 0.13, color by category with `hue="day", legend=False`; `palette=` without `hue=` now gives a warning.
concepts.code:
import matplotlib
matplotlib.use("Agg")
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt
import seaborn as sns
import pandas as pd
import numpy as np

rng = np.random.default_rng(2)
df = pd.DataFrame({
    "variant": np.repeat(["A", "B", "C"], 60),     # 60 rows per page version
    # np.r_[...] joins the three arrays of 60 times into one array of 180
    "time_s": np.r_[rng.normal(30, 5, 60), rng.normal(26, 4, 60), rng.normal(31, 9, 60)],
})

fig, (a, b) = plt.subplots(1, 2, figsize=(9, 3.5), layout="constrained")
sns.boxplot(data=df, x="variant", y="time_s", hue="variant", legend=False,
            fill=False, ax=a)
sns.stripplot(data=df, x="variant", y="time_s", color="0.3", alpha=0.5,
              size=3, ax=a)                        # raw dots on top of the boxes
sns.barplot(data=df, x="variant", y="time_s", order=["B", "A", "C"], ax=b)

for v in ["A", "B", "C"]:
    print(v, round(df[df["variant"] == v]["time_s"].mean(), 1))
# A 30.4
# B 25.9
# C 30.2   (the bar heights)
print([t.get_text() for t in b.get_xticklabels()])  # ['B', 'A', 'C']
fig.savefig("variants.png")
takeaways: Strip/swarm show every value, box/violin show the spread, bar/point show an estimate with its uncertainty
Use `order=` and `hue=` to control and split categories
Layer a strip plot over a box plot to show summary and data together
pitfalls: Passing values you already averaged to barplot, which then has nothing to compute an error bar from and draws a meaningless or missing one.

quiz.q: What does the height of a default `sns.barplot` bar represent?
options: The sum of the values in that category
The number of rows in that category
The mean of the values in that category, with an error bar showing a 95% confidence interval
quiz.explain: barplot averages each category by default and adds a 95% confidence interval; countplot is the one that counts rows.

concepts.name: Themes, contexts and color palettes
concepts.summary: Set the overall look with set_theme, scale text and lines for paper or a talk, and choose the right kind of color palette.
concepts.why: A consistent theme and the right kind of palette make charts readable and honest with almost no code.
concepts.body:
seaborn can change the look of all your charts in one line. `sns.set_theme()` switches every Matplotlib figure made after it to seaborn's defaults, which have three parts, each with its own argument:

- `style=`: background and grid, one of `"darkgrid"` (default), `"whitegrid"`, `"dark"`, `"white"`, `"ticks"`.
- `context=`: where the chart will be seen. `"paper"`, `"notebook"` (default), `"talk"` and `"poster"` make fonts and lines bigger step by step; `font_scale=1.2` adjusts further.
- `palette=`: the colors used in turn for each group or line (default `"deep"`).

The `context` setting is called the **plotting context**; pick `"talk"` for slides so text stays readable from the back of the room. The thin lines framing a plot area are its **spines**, and `sns.despine()` removes the top and right ones for a cleaner look.

To change the look for just a few lines of code, use `sns.axes_style("white")` or `sns.plotting_context("talk")` in a `with` block, the same way `with open(...)` keeps a file open only inside its block.

A **palette** is a set of colors, and the right kind depends on what the colors stand for:

- A **qualitative palette** for categories with no order: `"deep"`, `"colorblind"`, `"Set2"`, `"tab10"` give clearly different colors.
- A **sequential palette** for amounts, from light to dark: `"rocket"`, `"mako"`, `"viridis"`, `"Blues"`. seaborn uses one automatically when `hue` is numeric.
- A **diverging palette** for values on both sides of a middle point, like profit and loss around zero: `"vlag"`, `"icefire"`, `"RdBu"`.

`sns.color_palette("mako", 5)` returns a list of five colors, each stored as **RGB** amounts (how much red, green and blue it contains). You can reuse them in any Matplotlib call, and `as_cmap=True` returns a Matplotlib colormap instead.

A dict pins colors to categories: `palette={"control": "gray", "treatment": "C1"}` (`"C1"` is the second color of the current color cycle). Each category then keeps its color on every chart, whatever order the data comes in.

In anything others will read, use the `"colorblind"` palette and stay under about eight category colors; beyond that they become hard to tell apart.
concepts.code:
import matplotlib
matplotlib.use("Agg")
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt
import seaborn as sns
from matplotlib.colors import to_hex

sns.set_theme(style="whitegrid", context="talk", palette="colorblind")
print(plt.rcParams["font.size"])          # 18.0: Matplotlib's font size, enlarged by "talk"

pal = sns.color_palette("mako", 3)
print(len(pal), to_hex(pal[0]))           # 3 #3e356b
cmap = sns.color_palette("vlag", as_cmap=True)
print(type(cmap).__name__)                # ListedColormap (a Matplotlib colormap)

fig, ax = plt.subplots()
sns.barplot(x=["control", "treatment"], y=[3.1, 3.8],
            hue=["control", "treatment"],
            palette={"control": "gray", "treatment": "C1"}, ax=ax)
sns.despine()                             # remove the top and right frame lines
print(ax.spines["top"].get_visible())     # False
fig.savefig("themed.png")
takeaways: `set_theme` sets style, context and palette together
Contexts scale fonts and lines for paper, notebook, talk or poster
Qualitative palettes for categories, sequential for amounts, diverging around a middle point
pitfalls: Using a sequential palette (light to dark) for unordered categories, which suggests a ranking that does not exist.

quiz.q: You want consistent colors for 'control' and 'treatment' across ten different charts. What is the most robust choice?
options: Pass palette as a dict mapping each category to a color
Sort the data the same way each time
quiz.explain: A dict palette binds colors to category names, independent of order or which categories appear.

concepts.name: Axes-level vs figure-level functions
concepts.summary: Know the difference between functions that draw on one Axes and those that build whole multi-panel figures, and how to size and save each.
concepts.why: Mixing up the two is the top source of seaborn confusion: why `ax=` is ignored, why figsize does nothing, why the legend sits outside.
concepts.body:
seaborn has two kinds of plotting functions, and knowing which one you are calling explains most surprises.

**Axes-level** functions (`scatterplot`, `lineplot`, `histplot`, `kdeplot`, `boxplot`, `barplot`, `heatmap`, `regplot` ...) draw onto one Matplotlib Axes: the one you pass with `ax=`, or the current one. They return that Axes, so they fit into any layout you build with `plt.subplots`.

**Figure-level** functions create a whole new figure themselves, possibly with many panels, and return a grid object that manages it: a `FacetGrid` for most of them, a `PairGrid` or a `JointGrid` for the last two below. There is one per family:

- `relplot` (kind `"scatter"` / `"line"`),
- `displot` (`"hist"` / `"kde"` / `"ecdf"`),
- `catplot` (`"strip"`, `"box"`, `"violin"`, `"bar"`, ...),
- `lmplot`, `pairplot`, `jointplot`.

Their main extra is **faceting**: splitting the data into small multiples, one panel per value of a column. `col="region"` gives one panel per region side by side, `row="year"` one per year stacked, and `col_wrap=3` starts a new row of panels after every three.

Because they build the figure themselves, figure-level functions don't accept `ax=` and ignore `figsize`. Set each panel's size with `height=` (in inches) and `aspect=` (width divided by height). Their legend goes outside the panels by default.

The returned grid gives you `g.figure` (the whole figure), `g.axes` (a NumPy array of the panels' Axes), `g.axes_dict` (the same Axes looked up by facet value) and helpers: `g.set_axis_labels("x", "y")`, `g.set_titles("{col_name}")`, `g.set(xlim=...)`, `g.figure.suptitle(...)` and `g.savefig(...)`.

Rule of thumb: use figure-level functions to explore and split into panels quickly; use axes-level functions when placing a chart into a Matplotlib layout of your own.
concepts.code:
import matplotlib
matplotlib.use("Agg")
import seaborn as sns
import pandas as pd
import numpy as np

rng = np.random.default_rng(3)
df = pd.DataFrame({
    "x": rng.normal(size=300),
    "region": rng.choice(["north", "south", "east", "west"], 300),
    "plan": rng.choice(["free", "pro"], 300),
})
df["y"] = df["x"] * 2 + rng.normal(size=300)

g = sns.relplot(data=df, x="x", y="y", hue="plan", col="region",
                col_wrap=2, height=3, aspect=1.2)
g.set_titles("{col_name}")
g.set_axis_labels("Visits", "Spend")
print(type(g).__name__)                     # FacetGrid
print(g.axes.shape)                         # (4,)  col_wrap flattens the array
print(sorted(g.axes_dict))                  # ['east', 'north', 'south', 'west']
print(g.figure.get_size_inches().round())   # [8. 6.] (panels plus legend space)
g.savefig("facets.png")
takeaways: Axes-level functions take `ax=`; figure-level functions build their own figure
Figure-level functions facet with `col`, `row`, `col_wrap` and size with `height` and `aspect`
Customize grids through `g.figure`, `g.axes`, `g.set_titles` and `g.set_axis_labels`
pitfalls: Passing `ax=` or setting `plt.figure(figsize=...)` before `relplot`; both are ignored by figure-level functions.

quiz.q: You built `fig, axs = plt.subplots(1, 3)` and need a KDE plot in the third panel. Which call fits?
quiz.explain: Only axes-level functions draw into an existing Axes; displot always creates its own figure.

concepts.name: Aggregation and error bars
concepts.summary: Control how lineplot, barplot and pointplot combine repeated observations and what their error bars mean.
concepts.why: An error bar is a claim about your data; you must know whether it shows the spread of the data or the uncertainty of an estimate, and say which.
concepts.body:
When several rows share the same `x` (and the same `hue` group), `lineplot`, `barplot` and `pointplot` combine them into one number with an **estimator**, the summarizing function (the mean by default). Around that number they draw an interval chosen with `errorbar`:

- `("ci", 95)` (default): a 95% confidence interval, found by **bootstrapping**. seaborn redraws the group's rows at random, repeats allowed, a thousand times, recomputes the mean each time and keeps the range of the middle 95% of those means. It shrinks as you add data.
- `"se"`: the **standard error**, how much the mean would typically shift if you collected the data again; mean ± one standard error is roughly a 68% interval.
- `"sd"`: one standard deviation each way, showing the **spread** of the data itself; it does not shrink with more data.
- `("pi", 50)`: a percentile interval covering the middle 50% of the values (25th to 75th percentile).
- `None`: no interval, which also skips the bootstrap and is much faster on big data.

The first two describe how uncertain the estimate is; the last two describe how spread out the data is. Choose based on your question, and say which one you used in the caption.

Other settings:

- `estimator="median"`, or any function, such as `np.max`.
- `n_boot=` sets how many redraws the bootstrap makes, and `seed=` fixes its randomness so the figure comes out the same every run.
- With **repeated measures** (the same subject, such as a user, measured many times), `units="subject"` with `estimator=None` in `lineplot` draws one line per subject instead of combining them.
- `lineplot(err_style="bars")` draws error bars instead of a band.

If your data already has one row per x value, there is nothing to combine and no band is drawn. Any interval must then come from your own columns, plotted with Matplotlib's `fill_between` or `errorbar`.
concepts.code:
import matplotlib
matplotlib.use("Agg")
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt
import seaborn as sns
import pandas as pd
import numpy as np

rng = np.random.default_rng(4)
df = pd.DataFrame({
    "week": np.tile(np.arange(1, 9), 50),        # 50 users x 8 weeks
    "user": np.repeat(np.arange(50), 8),
})
df["minutes"] = 20 + 3 * df["week"] + rng.normal(0, 10, len(df))

fig, axs = plt.subplots(1, 3, figsize=(12, 3.5), sharey=True, layout="constrained")
for ax, eb in zip(axs, [("ci", 95), "sd", ("pi", 50)]):
    sns.lineplot(data=df, x="week", y="minutes", errorbar=eb, seed=0, ax=ax)
    ax.set_title(f"errorbar={eb}")

wk1 = df.loc[df.week == 1, "minutes"]
print(round(wk1.std(), 1), round(wk1.std() / np.sqrt(len(wk1)), 1))
# 11.2 1.6: sd describes spread, se/ci the precision of the mean
fig.savefig("errorbars.png")
takeaways: Repeated x values are combined with `estimator` (default mean)
`ci`/`se` show how uncertain the estimate is; `sd`/`pi` show the spread of the data
Set `seed=` for repeatable bootstrap intervals; `errorbar=None` for speed
pitfalls: Presenting a 95% confidence interval band as if it showed the range of individual values.

quiz.q: You add 10 times more users to the data. Which band gets substantially narrower?
quiz.explain: A confidence interval for the mean shrinks roughly with the square root of n; sd and percentile intervals describe the data's spread.

concepts.name: Heatmaps and pairwise plots
concepts.summary: Draw labeled heatmaps from pivot tables or correlation matrices, and explore every pair of columns with pairplot and jointplot.
concepts.why: Correlation matrices, pivot tables and a quick look at every variable pair are standard first steps in any exploration.
concepts.body:
A **heatmap** is a grid of colored cells, one per number, like a table you read by color. `sns.heatmap(table)` takes a 2D DataFrame (or array) and uses its index and columns as row and column labels. It is often fed a pivot table:

```python
table = df.pivot_table(index="weekday", columns="hour", values="orders", aggfunc="sum")
```

Another common input is a **correlation matrix**, `df.corr()`: for every pair of columns, how strongly they rise and fall together, from -1 to 1. The correlation of a with b equals that of b with a, so the matrix is a mirror image across its diagonal.

Useful arguments:

- `annot=True, fmt=".2f"` writes the values into the cells (`fmt="d"` for whole numbers).
- `cmap=` picks the colormap; for data around zero use a diverging one with `center=0`, so zero gets the neutral color. `vmin`/`vmax` fix the color range.
- `mask=` hides cells, for example the repeated upper-right half of a correlation matrix: `np.triu(np.ones_like(corr, dtype=bool))` is True on and above the diagonal.
- `square=True`, `linewidths=0.5`, `cbar_kws={"label": "..."}`.

`sns.clustermap` reorders rows and columns so similar ones sit next to each other. It uses **hierarchical clustering**: repeatedly join the two most similar rows (or columns) into a group until all are in one tree. It needs SciPy.

`sns.pairplot(df, hue="species")` builds a grid of every numeric column against every other: scatter plots off the diagonal and, on the diagonal, where a column would meet itself, that column's distribution. `corner=True` drops the repeated upper half, and `vars=[...]` picks the columns. With many columns it gets slow and unreadable; choose the relevant few.

`sns.jointplot(data=df, x=..., y=..., kind="scatter" | "hex" | "kde" | "reg")` shows a single pair, with each variable's own distribution along the top and right edges (its **marginal distributions**). It suits one important relationship.
concepts.code:
import matplotlib
matplotlib.use("Agg")
import seaborn as sns
import pandas as pd
import numpy as np

rng = np.random.default_rng(5)
df = pd.DataFrame(rng.normal(size=(300, 4)), columns=["a", "b", "c", "d"])
df["b"] += 0.8 * df["a"]                 # make b follow a
df["d"] -= 0.5 * df["c"]                 # make d move against c
df["group"] = rng.choice(["x", "y"], 300)

corr = df.drop(columns="group").corr()
mask = np.triu(np.ones_like(corr, dtype=bool))   # hide the diagonal and above
ax = sns.heatmap(corr, mask=mask, annot=True, fmt=".2f", cmap="vlag",
                 center=0, vmin=-1, vmax=1, square=True)
print(len(ax.texts))                     # 6: only the lower triangle annotated
ax.figure.savefig("corr.png")

g = sns.pairplot(df, hue="group", vars=["a", "b", "c"], corner=True)
print(type(g).__name__, g.axes.shape)    # PairGrid (3, 3)
g.savefig("pairs.png")
takeaways: Feed heatmap a pivot table or correlation matrix; index and columns become labels
Use `annot`, `center`, `vmin`/`vmax` and `mask` for readable matrices
`pairplot` scans all pairs; `jointplot` focuses on one, with marginal distributions
pitfalls: Running pairplot on 30 columns: 900 panels that take minutes and show nothing readable.

quiz.q: Why pass `mask=np.triu(np.ones_like(corr, dtype=bool))` to a correlation heatmap?
options: To hide the repeated upper triangle and the diagonal of 1s
To sort the variables by correlation
To speed up computing the correlation
To show only the strongest correlations
quiz.explain: A correlation matrix is a mirror image across its diagonal, so the upper triangle repeats the lower one; the mask hides it.

concepts.name: Regression plots: regplot and lmplot
concepts.summary: Overlay a fitted line with a confidence band, including curved, yes/no (logistic) and outlier-resistant fits.
concepts.why: A quick visual fit shows whether a relationship is roughly linear, curved or driven by outliers before you model it formally.
concepts.code:
import matplotlib
matplotlib.use("Agg")
import seaborn as sns
import pandas as pd
import numpy as np

rng = np.random.default_rng(6)
df = pd.DataFrame({"ads": rng.uniform(0, 10, 80)})
df["sales"] = 5 + 2.0 * df["ads"] + rng.normal(0, 3, 80)   # true line: 5 + 2 * ads
df["store"] = rng.choice(["mall", "street"], 80)

ax = sns.regplot(data=df, x="ads", y="sales", ci=95, seed=0,
                 scatter_kws={"alpha": 0.5})
slope, intercept = np.polyfit(df["ads"], df["sales"], 1)   # numbers come from you
print(round(slope, 1), round(intercept, 1))  # 2.0 4.8 (true: 2 and 5)
print(len(ax.collections))                   # 2: scatter points + confidence band
ax.figure.savefig("reg.png")

g = sns.lmplot(data=df, x="ads", y="sales", hue="store", height=3)
g.savefig("reg_by_store.png")
takeaways: regplot/lmplot draw a fitted line with a confidence band for the mean line
`order`, `logistic`, `robust` and `lowess` change the fitted model
They do not return the slope or other numbers; fit the model separately for those
pitfalls: Reading the narrow confidence band as the range where individual points will fall.

quiz.q: What does the shaded band around a regplot line represent?
options: The range containing 95% of the data points
A confidence interval for the regression line (the mean of y given x)
quiz.explain: The band is a bootstrap confidence interval for the fitted line, not a prediction interval for points.

concepts.name: Custom grids with FacetGrid and PairGrid
concepts.summary: Build your own faceted figures by mapping any plotting function over FacetGrid, PairGrid and JointGrid.
concepts.why: When no figure-level function does exactly what you need, the grid objects let you split any custom plot into panels.
concepts.body:
Figure-level functions are built on three grid objects you can also create yourself.

**FacetGrid** splits the data by `row`, `col` and `hue` and gives you one Axes per subset:

```python
g = sns.FacetGrid(df, col="region", hue="plan", height=3)
g.map_dataframe(sns.histplot, x="spend")
g.add_legend()
```

`g.map(func, "x", "y")` calls `func` once per subset with those columns as plain arrays, in order, which suits Matplotlib functions like `plt.scatter`. `g.map_dataframe(func, x="x", y="y")` passes `data=subset` plus your keywords, which suits seaborn functions.

Your own function works too, if it accepts `color` and `label` keywords and draws on `plt.gca()`, the Axes pyplot is currently drawing on (FacetGrid points it at each panel in turn).

Other useful methods: `g.refline(y=0)` draws a reference line in every panel, `g.set(xscale="log")` applies an Axes setting to all panels, `g.set_titles(col_template="{col_name}")` sets titles, and looping over `g.axes_dict.items()` lets you annotate panels one by one. `col_order` / `row_order` set the panel order.

**PairGrid** maps functions over all pairs of columns, with separate control of the diagonal and the two halves: `map_diag`, `map_lower` and `map_upper`, for example KDE contours below the diagonal and scatter plots above.

**JointGrid** gives a central plot plus marginal distributions: `g.plot_joint(...)` and `g.plot_marginals(...)`.

Faceting creates many Axes; keep facets to a few dozen and share axes (the default) so panels stay comparable.
concepts.code:
import matplotlib
matplotlib.use("Agg")
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt
import seaborn as sns
import pandas as pd
import numpy as np

rng = np.random.default_rng(7)
df = pd.DataFrame({"spend": rng.gamma(2, 20, 400),
                   "region": rng.choice(["eu", "us"], 400),
                   "plan": rng.choice(["free", "pro"], 400)})

def median_line(x, color=None, label=None, **kws):
    plt.gca().axvline(np.median(x), color=color, linestyle="--")

g = sns.FacetGrid(df, col="region", hue="plan", height=3, col_order=["us", "eu"])
g.map_dataframe(sns.histplot, x="spend", binwidth=10, alpha=0.5)
g.map(median_line, "spend")
g.add_legend()
g.set_titles(col_template="{col_name}")
print([ax.get_title() for ax in g.axes.flat])   # ['us', 'eu']
print(len(g.axes_dict["us"].lines))             # 2: one median line per plan

g.savefig("facet.png")
takeaways: FacetGrid draws one Axes per subset and maps any function across them
`map` passes columns as plain arrays; `map_dataframe` passes `data=` and keywords
PairGrid and JointGrid give separate control of diagonal, off-diagonal and marginal plots
pitfalls: Writing a custom mapped function that ignores the `color` keyword, so hue levels all share one color.

quiz.q: Which FacetGrid method should you use to map `sns.kdeplot` with `x='spend'`?
quiz.explain: map_dataframe passes the subset as data= with your keyword arguments, which is what seaborn functions expect.

concepts.name: Fine-tuning seaborn with Matplotlib
concepts.summary: Combine seaborn plots with Matplotlib layouts, legends, ticks and annotations to reach publication quality.
concepts.why: seaborn gets you 90% of the way; the last 10% (labels, layout, legends, highlights) is plain Matplotlib on the objects it returns.
concepts.body:
Because seaborn draws with Matplotlib, everything from the Matplotlib lessons applies to its output:

- An axes-level call returns an `Axes`: use `ax.set(xlabel=..., title=...)`, tick formatters, `ax.annotate`, `ax.axhline`.
- A figure-level call returns a grid: loop over `g.axes.flat`, or use `g.figure` for `suptitle` and layout.

seaborn's legend is a normal Matplotlib legend (`ax.get_legend()`). Reposition it with `sns.move_legend(obj, loc, title=None, ncols=3, frameon=False)`, which keeps the **legend handles** seaborn built: the small colored markers or lines beside each label. Calling `ax.legend()` again can lose them.

Combining several seaborn plots in one figure is just passing different `ax=` values from `plt.subplots` or `subplot_mosaic`, then calling `fig.savefig`. `layout="constrained"` keeps legends and labels from overlapping.

seaborn's themes work by changing **rcParams**, Matplotlib's dictionary of default settings. So `sns.set_theme` affects plain Matplotlib charts too, and Matplotlib **style sheets** (files of such settings) or `rc_context` affect seaborn. To use a seaborn style for one figure only, use `with sns.axes_style("white"):`.

seaborn adds artists in a known way: lines in `ax.lines`, bars in `ax.patches`, points in `ax.collections`. You can restyle one afterwards, for example to highlight one bar, though the exact order can change between versions; prefer parameters such as `hue` or `palette` when they exist.

Categorical axes place the categories at positions 0, 1, 2 ...; use those positions to place annotations.
concepts.code:
import matplotlib
matplotlib.use("Agg")
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt
from matplotlib import ticker
import seaborn as sns
import pandas as pd

df = pd.DataFrame({"team": ["data", "web", "ops", "ml"],
                   "share": [0.31, 0.27, 0.12, 0.30]})
fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(5, 3), layout="constrained")
sns.barplot(data=df, y="team", x="share", hue="team", legend=False,
            order=df.sort_values("share", ascending=False)["team"],
            palette={t: "C3" if t == "ml" else "0.7" for t in df.team}, ax=ax)
ax.xaxis.set_major_formatter(ticker.PercentFormatter(xmax=1))
for bars in ax.containers:                  # one container per hue level
    ax.bar_label(bars, fmt="{:.0%}", padding=3)
ax.set(xlabel="Share of incidents", ylabel=None, title="Incidents by team")
sns.despine(left=True)

print([t.get_text() for t in ax.get_yticklabels()])  # ['data', 'ml', 'web', 'ops']
print(len(ax.containers))                            # 4: one per hue level
fig.savefig("incidents.png")
takeaways: seaborn returns Axes or grids; finish them with ordinary Matplotlib calls
Use `sns.move_legend` instead of rebuilding seaborn legends
Compose several seaborn plots in one figure by passing `ax=`
pitfalls: Rebuilding the legend with `ax.legend()` after a seaborn plot and losing the hue and size handles.

quiz.q: A seaborn catplot legend overlaps the data. What is the most reliable fix?
options: Set legend=False and recreate it by hand
quiz.explain: move_legend relocates seaborn's legend while keeping its handles and title.

concepts.name: The seaborn.objects interface
concepts.summary: Build plots by combining a Plot with marks, stats and moves, in the style of the grammar of graphics.
concepts.why: seaborn.objects makes complex layered, faceted plots explicit and composable instead of hunting for function-specific parameters.
concepts.body:
Classic seaborn has one function per chart type, each with its own parameters. **seaborn.objects** (imported as `import seaborn.objects as so`) is a newer way to write plots, based on the **grammar of graphics**: any chart is data plus layers, and each layer says what to draw and what calculation to apply first. You describe the plot step by step in a `so.Plot`, and seaborn works out the drawing:

```python
(so.Plot(df, x="week", y="minutes", color="plan")
   .add(so.Line(), so.Agg())
   .add(so.Band(), so.Est(errorbar="se"))
   .facet(col="region")
   .label(x="Week", y="Minutes"))
```

The pieces:

- **Marks** decide what is drawn: `Dot`, `Dots`, `Line`, `Lines`, `Path`, `Bar`, `Bars`, `Area`, `Band`, `Range`, `Dash`, `Text`.
- **Stats** compute new data before drawing: `Agg` (the mean per x by default), `Est` (an estimate with an error interval), `Hist`, `KDE`, `Count`, `Perc` (percentiles), `PolyFit` (a fitted polynomial).
- **Moves** shift marks so they don't collide: `Dodge` (side by side), `Stack`, `Jitter`, `Shift`, `Norm` (rescale each group).
- **Plot methods**: `.add(mark, stat, move, **variables)` adds a layer, plus `.facet(col=, row=, wrap=)`, `.pair(x=[...])`, `.scale(...)`, `.limit(...)`, `.label(...)`, `.layout(size=...)`, `.theme({...})`, `.share(...)`.

Each method returns a new Plot and leaves the old one unchanged, so you can define a base plot and derive variants from it. Nothing is drawn until the plot is displayed in a notebook, shown with `.show()`, saved with `.save("file.png")`, or built without showing with `.plot()`.

Variables can be set on `Plot` for all layers or on a single `.add` call. `.on(ax)` or `.on(fig)` draws into an existing Matplotlib Axes or figure, so you can mix it with classic code.

seaborn 0.13 still marks seaborn.objects as experimental, but it covers most common plots.
concepts.code:
import matplotlib
matplotlib.use("Agg")
import seaborn as sns
import seaborn.objects as so
import pandas as pd
import numpy as np

rng = np.random.default_rng(8)
df = pd.DataFrame({"week": np.tile(np.arange(1, 7), 40),
                   "plan": np.repeat(["free", "pro"], 120),
                   "region": np.tile(np.repeat(["eu", "us"], 6), 20)})
df["minutes"] = 20 + 3 * df.week + (df.plan == "pro") * 8 + rng.normal(0, 6, 240)

base = so.Plot(df, x="week", y="minutes", color="plan")
p = (base.add(so.Line(marker="o"), so.Agg())
         .add(so.Band(), so.Est(errorbar="se"))
         .facet(col="region")
         .label(x="Week", y="Minutes per day")
         .layout(size=(8, 3.5)))
plotter = p.plot()                      # compile without showing
print(len(plotter._figure.axes))        # 2: one per region
p.save("objects.png")
print(type(base).__name__, base is p)   # Plot False: methods return new Plots
takeaways: Compose `so.Plot(...)` with `.add(mark, stat, move)` layers
Marks draw, stats compute new data, moves shift positions
Plot methods return new objects; nothing is drawn until shown, saved or plotted
pitfalls: Expecting `.add(...)` to modify a Plot in place; it returns a new Plot you must keep.

quiz.q: In `so.Plot(df, x='day', y='tip').add(so.Bar(), so.Agg())`, what does `so.Agg()` do?
options: Averages y per x (mean by default) before the bars are drawn
quiz.explain: Agg is a stat: it computes new data (here the mean per x) and the Bar mark draws the result.

concepts.name: How seaborn estimates: bootstrap and binning
concepts.summary: Understand exactly how seaborn computes confidence intervals, KDE bandwidths and histogram bins, and how to make them repeatable and fast.
concepts.why: Knowing the statistics behind the defaults lets you defend a figure, reproduce it exactly and avoid slow plots on large data.
concepts.body:
**Confidence intervals** in `barplot`, `pointplot`, `lineplot`, `regplot` and `so.Est` come from a nonparametric bootstrap, one that assumes no formula for the data's shape. seaborn **resamples** each group `n_boot` times (default 1000): it draws as many rows as the group has, at random and with replacement, so a row can be picked more than once. It recomputes the estimator on each resample and takes percentiles of those estimates (the 2.5th and 97.5th for 95%). Consequences:

- Results vary slightly from run to run unless you pass `seed=`.
- Cost grows with rows times `n_boot`; on millions of rows use `errorbar="se"` (computed by a formula for the mean, no resampling) or `None`.
- The bootstrap assumes independent rows: knowing one tells you nothing about another. With repeated measures, pass `units="subject"` so whole subjects are resampled instead of single rows, which gives honestly wider intervals.
- `weights=` (new in 0.13 for some functions) turns the estimator into a weighted mean.

**KDE bandwidth** comes from Scott's rule by default, a formula based on the data's spread and the number of values, used with a bell-shaped (Gaussian) kernel and then multiplied by `bw_adjust`. The rule fits data with one peak and no hard limits. Data with several peaks, or a hard edge such as prices that can't go below zero, needs a smaller `bw_adjust` or `cut=0`.

**Histogram bins** default to NumPy's `"auto"` rule. It computes two standard formulas, Sturges' (based only on the number of values) and Freedman-Diaconis' (based on the IQR and the count), and uses whichever gives more bins. `discrete=True` centers one bin on each whole number, which is right for counts.

When in doubt, reproduce the number yourself, as the example does, and check that the plot shows what you would report.
concepts.code:
import matplotlib
matplotlib.use("Agg")
import numpy as np
import pandas as pd
import seaborn as sns

rng = np.random.default_rng(9)
df = pd.DataFrame({"g": ["a"] * 200, "v": rng.exponential(10, 200)})

ax = sns.pointplot(data=df, x="g", y="v", errorbar=("ci", 95),
                   n_boot=2000, seed=42)
lo, hi = ax.lines[1].get_ydata()          # lines[0] is the point, [1] its CI
print(round(lo, 2), round(hi, 2))         # 9.03 12.1

# Reproduce a percentile bootstrap by hand
boot_rng = np.random.default_rng(42)
v = df["v"].to_numpy()
means = [boot_rng.choice(v, v.size).mean() for _ in range(2000)]
print(np.percentile(means, [2.5, 97.5]).round(2))   # very close to seaborn's
print(round(v.mean(), 2), round(v.std(ddof=1) / np.sqrt(v.size), 2))  # mean, se
takeaways: Default CIs are percentile bootstraps: `n_boot` resamples, then percentiles
Use `seed=` for repeatable results and `units=` for repeated measures
KDE uses Scott's rule times `bw_adjust`; bins default to NumPy's 'auto'
pitfalls: Bootstrapping single rows of repeated-measures data, which treats related rows as independent and gives too-narrow intervals.

quiz.q: Each of 20 subjects contributes 50 rows. Which option gives a more honest CI for the group mean in lineplot?
options: units='subject' so resampling happens per subject
quiz.explain: Resampling whole subjects respects the correlation within a subject; more bootstrap draws do not fix that.

concepts.name: Scales, properties and custom stats
concepts.summary: Control how data maps to visual properties with Scale objects, and extend seaborn.objects with your own Stat or Move.
concepts.why: Explicit scales and custom calculations let seaborn.objects express plots no built-in function supports.
concepts.body:
In seaborn.objects, each visual quality of a mark is a **property**: x, y, color, pointsize, linewidth, marker, alpha and so on. Every variable assigned to a property passes through a scale, the rule that turns data values into positions, colors or sizes. `.scale()` sets each one:

- `so.Continuous()` for numbers, with `.tick(...)` and `.label(like="{x:.0%}")`; or a string such as `.scale(y="log")` (also `"symlog"`, `"sqrt"`) to space the axis differently.
- `so.Nominal(order=[...])` for unordered categories, including numbers you want treated as categories: `.scale(color=so.Nominal(["#999", "C3"]))`.
- `so.Temporal()` for dates, `so.Boolean()` for True/False.
- A palette name, list or dict maps values to colors directly: `.scale(color="flare")`.

You can also skip scaling and give a fixed value: `.add(so.Dot(color="C3"))` paints every dot that color instead of mapping a variable to color.

To extend the system, write a subclass of `so.Stat` (it is a dataclass) and implement `__call__(self, data, groupby, orient, scales)`, returning a new DataFrame. `data` has columns named after properties (`x`, `y`, `color`...). `orient` is `"x"` or `"y"`: the axis that holds the groups. `groupby.apply(data, func)` runs `func` per group and keeps the grouping columns. A custom `so.Move` works the same way but changes positions.

Built-in stats use this same machinery, so custom ones work with facets, color groups and other layers. `so.Stat` and `so.Move` are only lightly documented and their details may still change, so pin your seaborn version when you rely on them.
takeaways: Every mapped property passes through a scale you can set with `.scale()`
Fixed mark arguments like `so.Dot(color='C3')` skip scaling
Subclass `so.Stat` and implement `__call__` to add your own calculations
pitfalls: Using a numeric column for color and getting a smooth range of shades when you meant separate categories; wrap the scale in `so.Nominal()`.

quiz.q: Your 'year' column holds integers 2024-2026 and you want three distinct colors, not a gradient. What do you do?
quiz.explain: Nominal tells seaborn to treat the values as unordered categories, giving distinct colors.

concepts.name: Large data and plotting performance
concepts.summary: Keep seaborn fast and readable on millions of rows by aggregating, binning, sampling and avoiding slow defaults.
concepts.why: Default seaborn settings that are fine on a thousand rows can take minutes or produce unreadable blobs on a million.
concepts.body:
Most seaborn slowness on big data comes from three sources.

**Bootstrapped error bars.** Each aggregated point redraws its group's rows `n_boot` times. With many groups and millions of rows this dominates. Use `errorbar=None` or `errorbar="se"`, or aggregate with pandas first and plot the summary with `errorbar=None`.

**One artist per point.** `scatterplot`, `stripplot` and especially `swarmplot` draw every observation. Placing a swarm takes time that grows with the square of the number of points (ten times the points, about a hundred times the work), so it becomes unusable beyond a few thousand points per category. Alternatives:

- 2D histograms: `sns.histplot(data=df, x=..., y=..., bins=50)` or Matplotlib's `hexbin`;
- distribution summaries: `boxenplot` (designed for large data) or `violinplot`;
- a random sample for the scatter layer, `df.sample(5_000, random_state=0)`, while statistics still use all rows.

**KDE on huge arrays.** `kdeplot` adds up one kernel per data point across a grid of positions; at this scale a histogram with many bins is much faster and shows the same shape.

Also, a `hue` column with hundreds of different values builds a huge legend and many artists; aggregate or filter first. Converting text columns to pandas' `category` type speeds up grouping and fixes their order.

Time the plot before and after each change: often one argument, such as `errorbar=None`, turns a minute-long plot into a second.
concepts.code:
import matplotlib
matplotlib.use("Agg")
import time
import numpy as np
import pandas as pd
import seaborn as sns
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt

rng = np.random.default_rng(10)
n = 200_000
df = pd.DataFrame({"x": rng.integers(0, 20, n), "g": rng.choice(list("abcd"), n)})
df["y"] = df.x * 0.5 + rng.normal(0, 3, n)

def timed(**kw):
    fig, ax = plt.subplots()
    t = time.perf_counter()
    sns.lineplot(data=df, x="x", y="y", hue="g", ax=ax, **kw)
    plt.close(fig)
    return time.perf_counter() - t

slow, fast = timed(n_boot=200), timed(errorbar=None)
print(fast < slow)                    # True: skipping the bootstrap is much faster

ax = sns.histplot(data=df, x="x", y="y", bins=(20, 40), cmap="mako")  # not a 200k scatter
ax.figure.savefig("big.png")
takeaways: Bootstraps dominate cost: use `errorbar=None` or 'se' on big data
Replace large scatters and swarms with 2D histograms, boxen plots or samples
Profile one change at a time; often one argument fixes the speed
pitfalls: Using swarmplot on tens of thousands of points, which is extremely slow and spills dots outside the category's space.

quiz.q: A lineplot over 5 million rows takes two minutes. Which change most likely helps most?
quiz.explain: The bootstrap redraws every group's rows many times; turning it off or aggregating first removes that cost.
